    96	Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
    97	introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.
    98	
    99	As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
   100	A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
   101	voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
   102	like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
   103	number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
   104	ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
   105	percentage of the total.
   106	
   107	Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
   108	respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
   109	instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.
   110	
   111	For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
   112	service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
   113	the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
   114	your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
   115	requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
   116	is reached.
   117	
   118	A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
   119	many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
   120	supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
   121	then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.
   122	
   123	The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
   124	as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).
   125	
   126	The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
   127	that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
   128	examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.
   129	
   130	[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
   131	do count against the budget.
   132	
   133	Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
   134	against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
   135	are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
   136	during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.
   137	
   138	It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
   139	to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
   140	The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
   141	before the drain can proceed.
   142	
   143	When a pod is evicted using the eviction API, it is gracefully
   144	[terminated](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination), honoring the
   145	`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting in its [PodSpec](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core).

    27	## Requests and limits
    28	
    29	If the node where a Pod is running has enough of a resource available, it's possible (and
    30	allowed) for a container to use more resource than its `request` for that resource specifies.
    31	
    32	For example, if you set a `memory` request of 256 MiB for a container, and that container is in
    33	a Pod scheduled to a Node with 8GiB of memory and no other Pods, then the container can try to use
    34	more RAM.
    35	
    36	Limits are a different story. Both `cpu` and `memory` limits are applied by the kubelet (and
    37	{{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}),
    38	and are ultimately enforced by the kernel. On Linux nodes, the Linux kernel
    39	enforces limits with
    40	{{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}}.
    41	The behavior of `cpu` and `memory` limit enforcement is slightly different.
    42	
    43	`cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
    44	its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
    45	container's limit. Thus, a `cpu` limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces.
    46	Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their `cpu` limit.
    47	
    48	`memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
    49	a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it. However,
    50	terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a
    51	container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means
    52	`memory` limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than
    53	its `memory` limit, but if it does, it may get killed.
    54	
    55	{{< note >}}
    56	There is an alpha feature `MemoryQoS` which attempts to add more preemptive
    57	limit enforcement for memory (as opposed to reactive enforcement by the OOM
    58	killer). However, this effort is
    59	[stalled](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/a47155b340/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos#latest-update-stalled)
    60	due to a potential livelock situation a memory hungry can cause.
    61	{{< /note >}}

   230	## How Pods with resource requests are scheduled
   231	
   232	When you create a Pod, the Kubernetes scheduler selects a node for the Pod to
   233	run on. Each node has a maximum capacity for each of the resource types: the
   234	amount of CPU and memory it can provide for Pods. The scheduler ensures that,
   235	for each resource type, the sum of the resource requests of the scheduled
   236	containers is less than the capacity of the node.
   237	Note that although actual memory
   238	or CPU resource usage on nodes is very low, the scheduler still refuses to place
   239	a Pod on a node if the capacity check fails. This protects against a resource
   240	shortage on a node when resource usage later increases, for example, during a
   241	daily peak in request rate.
   242	
   243	## How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits {#how-pods-with-resource-limits-are-run}
   244	
   245	When the kubelet starts a container as part of a Pod, the kubelet passes that container's
   246	requests and limits for memory and CPU to the container runtime.
   247	
   248	On Linux, the container runtime typically configures
   249	kernel {{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}} that apply and enforce the
   250	limits you defined.
   251	
   252	- The CPU limit defines a hard ceiling on how much CPU time the container can use.
   253	  During each scheduling interval (time slice), the Linux kernel checks to see if this
   254	  limit is exceeded; if so, the kernel waits before allowing that cgroup to resume execution.
   255	- The CPU request typically defines a weighting. If several different containers (cgroups)
   256	  want to run on a contended system, workloads with larger CPU requests are allocated more
   257	  CPU time than workloads with small requests.
   258	- The memory request is mainly used during (Kubernetes) Pod scheduling. On a node that uses
   259	  cgroups v2, the container runtime might use the memory request as a hint to set
   260	  `memory.min` and `memory.low`.
   261	- The memory limit defines a memory limit for that cgroup. If the container tries to
   262	  allocate more memory than this limit, the Linux kernel out-of-memory subsystem activates
   263	  and, typically, intervenes by stopping one of the processes in the container that tried
   264	  to allocate memory. If that process is the container's PID 1, and the container is marked
   265	  as restartable, Kubernetes restarts the container.
    45	## Prerequisites
    46	
    47	Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
    48	To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
    49	Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.

    51	## The two sorts of pod isolation
    52	
    53	There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
    54	They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
    55	means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
    56	restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
    57	independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.
    58	
    59	By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
    60	A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
    61	"Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
    62	When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
    63	the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
    64	allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    65	The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.
    66	
    67	By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
    68	A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
    69	has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
    70	When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
    71	the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
    72	the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    73	The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.
    74	
    75	Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
    76	pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
    77	what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.
    78	
    79	For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on
    80	the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If
    81	either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.

   203	For volume plugins that support the `Delete` reclaim policy, deletion removes

**Decision: revise before production approval.** The proposed fields provide useful controls, but do not establish five-replica availability, successful request draining, or database durability. Recommendations below are configuration choices unless identified as documented behavior. All source paths are relative to the supplied `docs/` directory; citations include source line ranges.

1. **PDB and rollout availability.** A PDB cannot prevent involuntary node failures; their unavailable Pods nevertheless consume its budget. During an eviction-based drain, `minAvailable: 5` permits one healthy replica’s eviction when six are healthy, then blocks further disruptive evictions until availability recovers. This depends on using the Eviction API, not direct deletion, and does not protect against concurrent failures. Deployment rolling updates are not constrained by PDBs. Consequently, `maxUnavailable: 2` permits rollout availability to fall to four. Recommend `maxUnavailable: 1`, `maxSurge: 1`, with capacity for surge Pods; use `maxUnavailable: 0` if preserving all six during planned updates warrants additional waiting. Neither configuration guarantees availability through simultaneous failures.  
   Sources: `concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:99–136`; `concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md:1189–1211`.

2. **Zone placement.** Configure topology spread using the API’s Pod selector, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, and `maxSkew: 1`, targeting two replicas per zone. The topology key identifies node labels whose equal values form domains. With `DoNotSchedule`, skew bounds the difference between the target domain’s matching-Pod count and the global minimum; violating placements remain unscheduled. `ScheduleAnyway` instead prefers reduced skew without enforcing the bound. For this API, prefer the latter if restoring serving capacity during zone loss outweighs strict balance. With strict placement, explicitly decide `minDomains`: setting three makes the global minimum zero when fewer than three eligible domains remain, potentially blocking replacements. Zone unavailability does not necessarily mean domain disappearance; eligibility and existing nodes matter. Constraints also do not guarantee continued balance after removals.  
   Sources: `concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:82–130,527–529,605–623`.

3. **Probes for slow startup.** Use a startup probe whose `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` covers measured worst-case initialization. Readiness and liveness begin only after startup succeeds. Configure readiness to reflect whether the API can serve requests, including indispensable database dependencies; readiness failure removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without itself restarting the container. Use liveness for conditions such as deadlock that restarting can remedy, rather than a temporary database outage. Startup or liveness failure reaching the configured threshold kills the container, with subsequent restart governed by its restart policy. These mechanisms do not prove that the chosen health checks accurately represent application health.  
   Sources: `tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md:311–318,342–358`; `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:479–497`.

4. **Termination and long requests.** The grace-period countdown starts **before** `preStop`; hook execution consumes that budget. Normally, the hook runs before the runtime sends TERM to the container’s main process. The kubelet requests a small, one-off two-second extension if the hook overruns; remaining processes face SIGKILL when termination expires. Endpoint updates occur concurrently with shutdown: terminating endpoints are not immediately removed from EndpointSlices, but have `ready: false` and are excluded from regular traffic; `serving` supports draining-aware consumers. Thirty seconds is a default, not a request-completion guarantee. Measure hook duration, request duration, and routing behavior, then configure sufficient grace and application signal handling.  
   Sources: `reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md:1008`; `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:581–639`.

5. **Resource sizing and CPU HPA.** Set explicit, measured CPU requests for every relevant container. Requests drive scheduling capacity checks and typically determine relative CPU allocation under contention; they are not usage ceilings. CPU limits impose throttling, potentially increasing request latency. Memory limits are enforced reactively through OOM killing, rather than equivalent CPU-style throttling; exceeding a memory limit need not trigger an immediate kill. Set memory requests and limits from measured workloads. Utilization-based HPA divides CPU usage by requested CPU: if relevant requests are missing from some containers, Pod CPU utilization is undefined and HPA cannot act on that metric.  
   Sources: `concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md:27–53,230–265`; `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:89–102`.

6. **HPA’s conservative adjustments.** HPA sets aside missing metrics and, for CPU, certain not-yet-ready Pods or samples predating readiness. Default readiness and CPU-initialization windows are 30 seconds and five minutes. For missing metrics, recalculation assumes 100% of target during downscale and 0% during upscale. Not-yet-ready Pods also contribute an assumed 0% when considering upscale, damping expansion. If recalculation reverses direction or falls within tolerance, scaling stops; default tolerance is 0.1. Downscale stabilization chooses the highest recommendation within the preceding window, defaulting to five minutes. Reported utilization excludes these conservative adjustments, so replica changes can differ from the apparent raw ratio. Validate startup behavior against the controller’s actual settings.  
   Source: `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:141–218`.

7. **Least-privilege networking.** Replace namespace default allowance with ingress and egress default-deny policies, then explicitly permit approved callers to the API port, API egress to the database port, and corresponding database ingress. Allow required DNS access to the cluster’s actual resolver endpoints and ports; Service-name discovery depends on DNS. Ingress and egress isolation are independent. Policies combine additively as a union, so an existing broad allow policy defeats a narrower intended restriction. Both source egress and destination ingress must permit a connection; reply traffic is implicitly allowed. A supporting CNI/network-policy implementation is a prerequisite: creating policy objects alone can have no effect. Test allowed and denied paths, including DNS.  
   Sources: `concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md:45–81,210–259`; `concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service.md:15–26`.

8. **Secrets and Git.** Base64 is insufficient protection: the documentation describes a base64 credential as “obscured but not secret.” Do not commit usable credentials merely because their Secret representation is encoded. Enable Secret encryption at rest; Secrets are otherwise stored unencrypted in etcd. Apply least-privilege RBAC and expose each Secret only to containers that require it. Restrict workload creation permissions too: someone authorized to create Pods, including indirectly through Deployments, can read any Secret in that namespace by arranging its consumption. Encryption at rest therefore does not replace authorization controls or protect a separately exposed Git copy.  
   Source: `concepts/configuration/secret.md:35–48,286–306,455–456`.

9. **Storage lifecycle.** Changing a StorageClass reclaim policy does not retroactively change existing PVs: the class supplies provisioning-time settings, and existing PVs must be edited or patched separately. `Retain` leaves a released PV and its data for manual reclamation after PVC deletion. With a supporting plugin, `Delete` removes both the PV and backing storage; dynamically provisioned volumes default to this unless configured otherwise. Active-use protection postpones PVC removal, not eventual reclamation. StatefulSet deletion or scaling normally retains its PVCs; optional `whenDeleted` and `whenScaled` retention settings can instead delete them, subsequently invoking PV reclamation. The supplied StatefulSet page identifies the feature-gate prerequisite. Prefer deliberate retention for database data, backed by recovery procedures.  
   Sources: `concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:34–36,126–135`; `concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:123–136,179–210`; `concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md:391–423`.

10. **Prioritized rollout and validation checklist.**

   - **Before deployment:** remove encoded credentials from the proposed Git workflow; verify encryption, RBAC, workload-creation permissions, CNI enforcement, existing PV reclaim policies, and StatefulSet retention settings. These controls have separate prerequisites and lifecycle effects, as documented in questions 7–9.
   - **Before traffic:** configure probes, measured resource requests, a conservative rollout, zone placement, and adequate grace. Reserve surge and failure-recovery capacity. For topology-constrained storage, consider supported `WaitForFirstConsumer` provisioning; immediate binding can leave Pods unschedulable (`concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:171–195`).
   - **Before approval:** exercise drain, rolling update, node/zone loss, cold startup, missing metrics, database outage, long-request termination, and restore scenarios. Validate at least four limits the cited mechanisms do not establish: application health-check accuracy, maximum successful drain duration, sufficient surviving-zone capacity, and database recovery correctness. Also establish whether CPU utilization predicts API demand. PDB scope, scheduling limitations, forced termination, and HPA adjustments explicitly prevent treating field configuration as an end-to-end availability guarantee (`concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:130–136`; `concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:605–623`; `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:619–639`; `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:183–218`).
